title: Simulation of a Battery Cell on Quantum Computers: Reactions & Transport
authors: Albert J. Pool, Michael Schelling, Birger Horstmann
abstract: Simulations of electrochemical materials and systems accelerate technological progress, but are still limited by computational power. In particular, quantum computing offers prospects for higher resolutions, due to the exponential amount of data that can be stored in a quantum state. As current quantum computers are still noisy, we consider a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, that divides the problem into smaller computational tasks. We describe how to implement such an algorithm for non-linear partial differential equations, the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian, in a scalable way for an electrochemical system. We show how it can evaluate general electrochemical models and present a quantum simulation of the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) as the first quantum simulation of a battery cell.
summary: This paper tackles the computational challenge of simulating battery cells by mapping the governing non-linear PDEs onto a quantum circuit framework. They propose and demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm using the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian to achieve the first quantum simulation of the SPMe model. This work shows a viable pathway for quantum computation to accelerate materials science simulations.
main_problem: Simulating complex electrochemical materials and systems, like battery cells, which are computationally limited by classical methods.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the first quantum simulation of a battery cell using the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) via a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm is employed, utilizing the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian to encode the non-linear partial differential equations governing charge transport and reactions.
model_or_system: The system is a battery cell modeled by the SPMe, involving coupled non-linear PDEs for concentration and potential. The physics is encoded into a Hamiltonian structure suitable for quantum circuit implementation.
key_observables: Cell voltage (U), solid concentration (c_s,k), and electrochemical potential ($\phi_k$).
important_parameters: Diffusion coefficients ($D_{s,k}$), particle radii ($R^*_k$), and current density ($j_k$).
main_assumptions: The use of a hybrid quantum-classical approach is necessary due to current quantum hardware noise (NISQ era).
figures_summary: Figures show the evolution of concentration and potential during charging and GITT cycles, comparing quantum simulation results to established numerical solutions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the computational bottleneck, details the adaptation of the SPMe equations into a quantum Hamiltonian formulation, describes the hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, and validates the method by simulating charging and GITT cycles.
why_interesting: It represents a direct application of quantum computing principles (Hamiltonian encoding, variational algorithms) to solve complex, time-dependent, non-linear partial differential equations arising in condensed matter electrochemistry.
